title: Bagtech (Apr 2012 TCC) Tax Court of Canada SR&ED Case
subject: Tax Court case examining whether a unanimous shareholder agreement affected CCPC status for enhanced SR&ED credits.
summary: In Bagtech (2012 TCC 120), the Tax Court of Canada ruled that a CBCA corporation whose voting shares were more than 60% non-resident-owned remained a Canadian-controlled private corporation, because its unanimous shareholders' agreement prevented non-residents from electing a board majority. Foreign-backed Canadian innovators can therefore preserve refundable 35% SR&ED investment tax credits through properly drafted governance.
metaDescription: Discover the April 2012 Tax Court of Canada ruling for Bagtech regarding Canadian SR&ED investment tax credit eligibility.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural History and Factual Context of the Taxpayer's Claim

In Price Waterhouse Coopers Inc., Acting in the Capacity of Trustee in Bankruptcy of Bioartificial Gel Technologies (BAGTECH) Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2012 TCC 120; Docket: 2009-3734(IT)G), rendered on April 12, 2012, the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) adjudicated a foundational dispute governing the eligibility of foreign-financed Canadian technology enterprises for enhanced, refundable Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Investment Tax Credits (ITCs). Bioartificial Gel Technologies (BAGTECH) Inc. ("Bagtech") was incorporated on March 8, 1996, under the Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA) and operated as a "taxable Canadian corporation" within the meaning of subsection 89(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) (ITA). Specializing in advanced biomedical technologies—specifically moist wound-healing hydrogel bandages—Bagtech engaged in intensive scientific research and experimental development activities throughout its 2004 and 2005 taxation years, which ended on December 31, 2004, and December 31, 2005, respectively.

During the 2004 taxation year, Bagtech incurred $1,017,722 in qualified SR&ED current operating expenses and $431,517 in qualified SR&ED capital expenditures. During the 2005 taxation year, the corporation incurred an additional $1,461,189 in qualified SR&ED operating expenses and $69,641 in qualified SR&ED capital expenditures. Bagtech filed amended prescribed SR&ED forms for both taxation years claiming status as a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" (CCPC) pursuant to subsection 125(7) of the ITA. Qualification as a CCPC was financially significant for Bagtech because, having concluded that Bagtech was not a CCPC, the Minister treated it as a "non-qualifying corporation" within the meaning of subsection 127(9) of the ITA that was not entitled to the "refundable investment tax credit" provided for in subsection 127.1(1) of the ITA. Under subsections 127(10.1) and 127.1(1) of the ITA, a corporation that qualifies as a CCPC throughout the taxation year is entitled to an enhanced 35% ITC rate—comprising the base 20% rate under subsection 127(9) plus the additional 15% CCPC rate under subsection 127(10.1)—and, crucially, cash refundability of up to 100% of credits earned on current SR&ED expenditures and 40% on capital SR&ED expenditures within its annual expenditure limit. Conversely, a private corporation that fails to qualify as a CCPC is classified as a "non-qualifying corporation" and is restricted to a non-refundable 20% ITC that can only be carried forward or back to offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable.

To finance its biomedical R&D operations, Bagtech completed successive rounds of equity financing involving Canadian institutional funds, foreign venture capital corporations, and "business angels" (two European business angels in 1999 and, in 2003, Youri Popowski of Geneva and Investissements Onami inc. of Quebec). Bagtech's authorized share capital consisted of Class A, B, C, D, and E shares, of which only Class A shares carried voting and participating rights. Classes B and C were non-voting shares bearing a non-cumulative dividend at a maximum rate of 8% and redeemable for their stated capital amount, while Classes D and E were non-voting shares bearing a maximum 8% non-cumulative dividend and redeemable at their stated amount plus a premium equal to the difference between the stated amount and the fair market value of property contributed upon issuance. Throughout the 2004 and 2005 taxation years, apart from a single non-voting Class D share issued at incorporation to Canadian resident founder Guy Fortier in exchange for contributed technologies, all issued and outstanding shares of Bagtech were voting Class A shares. As foreign equity participation expanded, the proportion of Class A voting shares held collectively by non-residents of Canada rose from 45.31% in 2002 to over 60% as of December 31, 2004, and reached 70.42% as of December 31, 2005.

However, on September 11, 2003, all of Bagtech's shareholders executed a written Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement (USA) under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA to govern the internal management and board representation of the corporation. Under Articles 3.1 and 3.2 of the 2003 USA, the shareholders agreed to exercise their voting rights to elect and maintain a Board of Directors of seven members allocated across three defined shareholder groups. Group A—composed of the founders (Marie-Pierre Faure, Guy Fortier, Richard J. Deckelbaum, Jean Emmanuel Raphael Guetta, Richard Émile Azera with Amaze, and Jean-François Brisson), Marie-Claude Lévesque, Marielle Robert, Youri Popowski, and Investissements Onami inc., a group that included several non-residents of Canada (Deckelbaum of New York, Guetta of London, Amaze and Azera of Brussels, and Popowski of Geneva) but whose directors the Court found were elected by residents of Canada—was entitled to elect two directors, including Marie-Pierre Faure. Group B—composed of venture capital entities SGF, FSTQ, FRSIM, Finedix, and Auriga—was entitled to elect three directors, of which Canadian resident entities FSTQ and FRSIM jointly appointed one director, Canadian resident SGF appointed one director, and non-resident Auriga appointed one director. Group C—composed of non-resident institutional investors Medco, Gutrafin, and Schroder—was entitled to elect two directors, including André Lamotte, while Collin Bier, a director appointed by the Group C shareholders, was to act as Chair of the Board of Directors under paragraph 3.2 of the USA for as long as the majority of the shareholders so agreed. Following additional share subscriptions in July 2005 by HSBC, Auxitec, Ayman, and Bagadine, Articles 3.1 and 3.2 of the USA were amended on July 22, 2005, to expand the Board from seven to eight directors by granting Group C a third director appointed by non-resident Bagadine. Consequently, notwithstanding that non-residents held over 60% (in 2004) and 70.42% (in 2005) of the voting Class A shares on the share register, the USA contractually and constitutionally restricted non-resident shareholders to appointing only three of seven directors (42.86%) throughout 2004 and from January 1 to July 21, 2005, and four of eight directors (50.00%) from July 22 to December 31, 2005.

body.text: After filing, on or about June 1, 2007, amended prescribed forms seeking CCPC status and refundable investment tax credits at the 35% rate instead of the 20% rate initially claimed, Bagtech made an assignment of property on October 21, 2008, and Price Waterhouse Coopers Inc. (PwC) was appointed trustee in bankruptcy. Shortly thereafter, on November 3, 2008, the Minister of National Revenue ("Minister"), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), issued its formal decision denying Bagtech CCPC status for the 2004 and 2005 taxation years and disallowing the refundable 35% SR&ED ITCs, followed on April 9, 2009, by Notices of Determination of Loss. PwC, in its capacity as trustee in bankruptcy, appealed the determinations to the Tax Court of Canada under the General Procedure.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Litigating Positions

The CRA did not dispute the underlying scientific eligibility of Bagtech's hydrogel research under subsection 248(1) of the ITA or the dollar quantum of the qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in 2004 and 2005. Instead, the Crown challenged the claim strictly on corporate control grounds under paragraph (b) of the definition of "Canadian-controlled private corporation" in subsection 125(7) of the ITA. The Minister advanced a primary argument and, in the alternative, two further submissions (paragraph 3 of the reasons), consistent with the CRA's administrative position, set out in Technical Interpretation 2008-0265902I7 (May 6, 2008) and at the 2009 Canadian Tax Foundation CRA Round Table, that a USA has no impact on the second stage of the paragraph 125(7)(b) analysis.

First, the Crown argued that Unanimous Shareholders' Agreements cannot be taken into consideration at all when applying the "hypothetical shareholder" test in paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA. Under the two-stage test established by the Federal Court of Appeal in Sedona Networks Corp. v. The Queen (2007 FCA 169), all shares owned by non-resident persons and public corporations are notionally aggregated and attributed to a single hypothetical "particular person" at Stage 1, followed by an assessment at Stage 2 of whether that hypothetical "particular person" exercises de jure control over the corporation. The Minister contended that Stage 2 is a purely arithmetical calculation governed strictly by voting share ownership on the corporate share register. Because the "particular person" is a statutory fiction created by the ITA rather than an actual signatory to the USA, the Crown argued that the hypothetical person is unbound by the USA's voting restrictions and that taking a USA into account at Stage 2 would skew the statutory control test.

Second, in the alternative, the Crown contended that even if a constitutional USA under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA can be examined in a de jure control analysis pursuant to the Supreme Court of Canada's landmark decision in Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. The Queen ([1998] 1 S.C.R. 795), the clauses genuinely in the nature of a USA (that is, those restricting the directors' powers) did not operate to withdraw de jure control from the non-resident shareholders who together formed the majority (paragraph 3(a) of the reasons). In addressing the USA, the Court itself examined whether such an agreement is divisible, that is, whether, as some authors maintain, only the clauses restricting the directors' powers are governed by the USA provisions of the CBCA, while clauses on other matters, such as the election of directors, are not. Reviewing doctrine (notably Paul Martel and Daniel Lafortune) and the Quebec Superior Court's decision in Leblanc v. Fertek Inc. (REJB 2000-20884), where Dalphond J. treated the management clauses of a shareholders' agreement differently from its clauses on the ownership and transfer of shares (in a corporate-law dispute rather than a control analysis), the Court considered whether the clauses governing the election of directors (Articles 3.1 and 3.2 of Bagtech's USA) had to be excluded from the de jure control analysis.

Third, also in the alternative, the Crown submitted that, even if the USA were taken into consideration, de jure control was not withdrawn from the non-resident majority shareholders because a majority of the clauses in the USA provided that they would be implemented by ordinary resolution, so that the non-residents controlled the decision-making in relation to those clauses (paragraph 3(b) of the reasons); on this view, nothing in the USA operated to strip de jure control from the non-resident majority, leaving the non-resident majority (>60% in 2004 and 70.42% in 2005) in overall legal control of the corporation.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework in Canada

The adjudication of Bagtech's entitlement to refundable SR&ED tax credits rested on the precise interaction between federal income tax provisions, federal corporate law statutes, and Supreme Court of Canada jurisprudence on corporate control. Under subsection 125(7) of the ITA, a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" is defined as a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than a corporation controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons or public corporations under paragraph 125(7)(a), or a corporation that "would, if each share of the capital stock of a corporation that is owned by a non-resident person, by a public corporation (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), or by a corporation described in paragraph (c) were owned by a particular person, be controlled by the particular person" under paragraph 125(7)(b). This CCPC definition feeds directly into the SR&ED investment tax credit regime under subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), and 127.1(1) of the ITA, which establish the statutory mechanism whereby a corporation that qualifies as a CCPC throughout a taxation year earns an additional 15% ITC on its qualified SR&ED expenditure pool (up to its annual expenditure limit, yielding a 35% combined credit) and qualifies as a "qualifying corporation" eligible for refundable ITCs under subsection 127.1(1).

The corporate law dimension of the dispute turned on section 146 of the CBCA, in particular subsections 146(1) and 146(3), as contrasted with ordinary voting agreements among shareholders, which section 145.1 of the CBCA separately recognizes. Section 145.1 of the CBCA recognizes ordinary written voting agreements between two or more shareholders providing that in exercising voting rights, the shares held by them shall be voted as provided in the agreement. In contrast, subsection 146(1) of the CBCA defines a Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement as an otherwise lawful written agreement among all the shareholders of a corporation, or among all the shareholders and one or more persons who are not shareholders, that restricts, in whole or in part, the powers of the directors to manage, or supervise the management of, the business and affairs of the corporation. Furthermore, subsection 146(2) recognizes a written declaration by a sole beneficial shareholder that similarly restricts the directors' powers as a USA, and subsection 146(3) of the CBCA mandates that a person who becomes a holder of shares that are subject to a USA is deemed to be a party to that agreement.

In interpreting how these corporate provisions govern "control" under the ITA, the Tax Court of Canada synthesized three foundational lines of Canadian appellate authority. First, in Buckerfield's Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue ([1965] 1 Ex. C.R. 299; 64 DTC 5301), President Jackett of the Exchequer Court established that "control" in the ITA contemplates de jure control—rather than de facto control—defined as the ownership of such a number of shares as carries with it the right to a majority of the votes in the election of the board of directors. The Supreme Court of Canada repeatedly affirmed the Buckerfield's rule across Dworkin Furs (Pembroke) Ltd., Vina-Rug (Canada) Ltd., and Imperial General Properties Ltd.. Second, in Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. The Queen ([1998] 1 S.C.R. 795; 98 DTC 6334), Justice Iacobucci speaking for the Supreme Court of Canada clarified that while external commercial or voting agreements are excluded from de jure control (being relevant only to de facto control under subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA), a statutory USA under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA is "a corporate law hybrid, part contractual and part constitutional in nature" (para. 66). Because a shareholder's de jure control depends in a very real way on the control enjoyed by the majority of directors whose election lies within that shareholder's control, any constitutional agreement altering the power to elect the board or the board's legal authority to manage the corporation necessarily alters the reality of de jure control. Accordingly, at paragraph 85 of Duha Printers, the Supreme Court held that in determining de jure control, courts must examine the corporation's governing statute, its share register, its constating documents, and any Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement to ascertain whether there is any specific or unique limitation on either the majority shareholder's power to control the election of the board or the board's power to manage the business and affairs of the company. Third, in Sedona Networks Corp. v. The Queen (2007 FCA 169) and R. v. Verrette ([1978] 2 S.C.R. 838), the Federal Court of Appeal (in Sedona Networks) established that paragraph 125(7)(b) requires a two-stage attribution and control analysis, while the Supreme Court of Canada (in Verrette) characterized a deeming provision as a statutory fiction; drawing on Verrette, Attorney General of Canada v. Scarola (2003 FCA 157) and Survivance v. Canada (2006 FCA 129), Justice Bédard concluded that the legal effects of the paragraph 125(7)(b) fiction are superimposed on the truth being pushed aside, so that the "particular person" has the same rights and is subject to the same obligations as the non-resident owners of the shares.
The Tax Court of Canada's Holding and Subsequent Appellate Affirmation

Justice Paul Bédard allowed Bagtech's appeal with costs for both the 2004 and 2005 taxation years, holding that Bagtech was a CCPC within the meaning of subsection 125(7) of the ITA during the 2004 and 2005 taxation years and, therefore, was entitled to the "refundable investment tax credit" provided for in subsection 127.1(1) of the ITA.

In rejecting the Minister's primary argument, Justice Bédard held that the statutory fiction in paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA does not strip the aggregated shares of their existing legal rights and constitutional restrictions. Applying R. v. Verrette together with Attorney General of Canada v. Scarola (2003 FCA 157), Survivance v. Canada (2006 FCA 129) and subsection 146(3) of the CBCA, the Court reasoned, relying on the French doctrine quoted in Scarola, that a legal fiction operates by misrepresenting the facts—treating multiple non-resident shareholders as a single hypothetical "particular person"—and extracting the legal consequences that flow from that supposition while leaving all other uncontradicted legal truths intact. Consequently, when all non-resident shares are notionally attributed to the hypothetical "particular person" at Stage 1 of the Sedona Networks test, that hypothetical person is deemed to possess the exact same rights and be subject to the exact same obligations as the actual non-resident owners of the shares, including being bound as a deemed party to the USA under subsection 146(3) of the CBCA.

Justice Bédard then addressed whether the clauses of the USA governing the election of directors (Articles 3.1 and 3.2) must be taken into account, even though he agreed with Robert Couzin's interpretation of Duha Printers and with his criticism of that decision, and acknowledged doctrine and Quebec case law treating a USA as severable. In Appendix 3 of the reasons, the Court identified the provisions of Bagtech's September 11, 2003 agreement that expressly limit the directors' powers (paragraphs 3.2, 3.4.1, 3.4.3, 4.2, 4.3, 10.2, 11.5, 13.4, and 18.1), listed paragraph 13.1 separately as a provision in the nature of a USA under subsection 6(3) of the CBCA because it raises the shareholder vote required for certain measures, and characterized those clauses as minor restrictions on the directors' powers that did not, in themselves, operate to strip the hypothetical shareholder of de jure control (paragraph 87). Once an agreement qualifies as a constitutional USA under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA, paragraph 85 of Duha Printers requires, on the Court's careful reading (which it acknowledged produces an "unusual result" that it was nonetheless bound to follow), the court to give effect to any specific or unique limitation manifested in the USA on "the majority shareholder's power to control the election of the board". Because Articles 3.1 and 3.2 of the USA permitted the hypothetical non-resident shareholder to elect only three out of seven directors in 2004 and from January 1 to July 21, 2005, and four out of eight directors from July 22 to December 31, 2005 (residents of Canada electing four directors throughout), the hypothetical person could not elect a majority of the Board of Directors and therefore lacked de jure control. The reasons do not, however, contain any finding on whether the non-resident majority could amend or terminate the USA; the Court did not address that question (clause 15.2 of the USA provides for termination by consent of the Shareholders, and, unlike subsection 146(8) of the Alberta Business Corporations Act reproduced in Appendix 2, the CBCA provisions quoted in the reasons contain no express unanimity rule for amendments).

On subsequent appeal by the Crown in Her Majesty the Queen v. Price Waterhouse Coopers Inc., Acting in the Capacity of Trustee in the Bankruptcy of Bioartificial Gel Technologies (BAGTECH) Inc. (2013 FCA 164), the Federal Court of Appeal (Reasons for Judgment delivered by Justice Johanne Gauthier) unanimously affirmed Justice Bédard's decision. The Federal Court of Appeal confirmed the full scope of Duha Printers, holding that voting provisions regarding the election of directors contained within a lawful CBCA Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement must be given full legal effect in the de jure control analysis under paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA, thereby cementing Bagtech as the governing Canadian authority on CCPC eligibility for SR&ED tax incentives.
Core Legal, Contractual, and Evidentiary Vulnerabilities

Although the Trustee in Bankruptcy ultimately prevailed before the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal, the underlying dispute in Bagtech exposed severe legal, structural, and documentation vulnerabilities. In practical terms, the dispute meant that Bagtech's claim to refundable SR&ED tax credits, made on or about June 1, 2007, remained unresolved when Bagtech made an assignment of property on October 21, 2008, before the CRA issued, on November 3, 2008, its decision that Bagtech was not a CCPC, although the reasons do not attribute the bankruptcy to the tax dispute. A rigorous examination of the ruling—combined with the broader statutory architecture of the Canadian SR&ED regime—identifies five core legal, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls that Canadian tax practitioners must address.
Equity Dilution Without Constitutional Share Class Segregation

The initial catalyst for the CRA's reassessment was Bagtech's reliance on a single voting share class (Class A) across successive foreign venture capital and angel financing rounds. While Bagtech's articles of incorporation authorized Class A, B, C, D, and E shares, classes B through E were structured strictly as non-voting preferred shares bearing an 8% non-cumulative dividend, and only a single Class D share was issued and outstanding throughout the 2004 and 2005 taxation years. Every equity investor—whether Canadian resident founder, Quebec institutional fund (SGF, FSTQ, FRSIM), or non-resident venture capital fund (Auriga, Medco, Gutrafin, Schroder, Bagadine)—received identical Class A voting shares.

When non-resident ownership crossed the 50% threshold—reaching over 60% in 2004 and 70.42% in 2005—Bagtech's T2 corporate income tax return and prescribed SR&ED filings automatically presented a prima facie arithmetic violation of paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA on the face of the corporate share register. In Canadian tax administration, CRA financial reviewers routinely evaluate CCPC status at the initial desk-audit stage by inspecting the share register and Articles of Incorporation. Because Bagtech did not embed differential voting rights or class-specific director election mechanics—such as separate Class A Canadian-resident voting shares and Class B non-resident limited-voting shares—directly into its Articles of Incorporation, its CCPC status depended entirely on defeating the CRA's entrenched administrative policy against recognizing USAs under paragraph 125(7)(b), virtually guaranteeing a protracted dispute with the CRA Appeals Division and the Department of Justice.
The Hybrid Nature of Unanimous Shareholders' Agreements: Section 145.1 Versus Section 146(1) CBCA

The most perilous legal pitfall illuminated in Bagtech lies in the thin statutory boundary between an ordinary voting agreement under section 145.1 of the CBCA and a constitutional Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA. Under Duha Printers, an ordinary shareholders' agreement—even if signed unanimously by 100% of the shareholders—is treated as a purely private contractual instrument that is legally irrelevant to de jure control. If a shareholders' agreement merely contains voting covenants for the election of directors (for example, stipulating that Shareholder Group A shall elect four directors and Shareholder Group B shall elect three directors) without simultaneously restricting the statutory powers of the directors to manage the business and affairs of the corporation under the CBCA, the agreement fails to qualify as a USA under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA.

In Bagtech, the Court itself identified, in Appendix 3 of Justice Bédard's reasons, the clauses of the September 11, 2003 agreement that genuinely restrict the directors' powers (the parties not disputing, as the Federal Court of Appeal later noted, that Appendix 3 is an exhaustive list and that the agreement is a USA), while characterizing those restrictions as minor ones that did not, in themselves, strip the hypothetical shareholder of de jure control (paragraph 87). Specifically, Paragraph 3.2 of the USA divested the directors of their ordinary statutory power to choose the Chair of the Board, mandating that Collin Bier act as Chair so long as a majority of the shareholders agreed. Subparagraph 3.4.1 constrained the Board's procedural discretion by mandating that directors hold at least six Board meetings per year with no more than two months elapsing between meetings, while Subparagraph 3.4.3 restricted the Board's ability to transact business by requiring the presence of a representative from each of Group A, Group B, and Group C to form a valid quorum. Paragraphs 4.2 and 4.3 stripped the directors of discretion over share transfers by forcing them to authorize transfers in specified situations regardless of charter or bylaw provisions. Furthermore, Paragraph 10.2 removed the Board's strategic autonomy over corporate liquidity events by mandating the retention of a commercial bank of international repute—selected by a majority vote of Institutional Shareholders—to study strategic options if a public share offering or asset/share sale had not occurred by December 31, 2008. Paragraphs 11.5 and 18.1 transferred the decision-making power over whether redeemed shares upon a shareholder's death, permanent incapacity, or bankruptcy/insolvency would be purchased personally by co-shareholders or redeemed by the corporation from the Board to the co-shareholders acting by majority vote. Finally, Paragraph 13.4 prohibited the Board from issuing any security without the prior express agreement of shareholders representing at least 50% of the capital stock on an undiluted basis, while Paragraph 13.1, which the Court listed separately as a provision in the nature of a USA under subsection 6(3) of the CBCA rather than as a restriction of the directors' powers, elevated the shareholder voting threshold to a three-quarters (75%) supermajority for numerous corporate measures that would ordinarily require only a two-thirds special resolution under subsection 2(1) of the CBCA. Had Bagtech's agreement lacked these Appendix 3 management-restricting clauses—or had the agreement failed to include every single shareholder, including Guy Fortier, who held 547,610 Class A shares as well as the sole non-voting Class D share, since subsection 146(1) of the CBCA requires a written agreement among all shareholders, voting and non-voting alike—the agreement would have been classified as a mere section 145.1 voting contract, and, in light of paragraph 82 of the reasons (under which a restriction on the election of directors is not relevant if it appears in a mere voting agreement), its director-election clauses would not have been taken into account in the de jure control analysis.
Ordinary Resolution Traps and Unilateral Amendment Vulnerabilities

A critical secondary vulnerability targeted by the Minister in Bagtech was the pervasive use of "ordinary resolution" thresholds (50% plus one vote of shareholders) inside the USA to implement transferred management decisions. In many venture-backed USAs, powers removed from the Board of Directors under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA are vested in the shareholders acting by ordinary resolution. However, if a USA strips core management powers from the Board and vests them in the shareholders acting by simple majority vote, and non-residents own >60% or 70.42% of the voting shares, the hypothetical non-resident "particular person" acquires direct legal authority to manage the corporation in place of the Board. Under Duha Printers, where a USA provides that the legal authority to manage the corporation lies other than with the Board, the reality of de jure control is altered and follows that management authority.

The reasons do not contain a separate analysis of this ordinary-resolution argument: the Court found that the clauses genuinely in the nature of a USA listed in Appendix 3 (such as the retention of a bank selected by a majority vote of the Institutional Shareholders under Paragraph 10.2, or shareholder approval of security issuances under Paragraph 13.4) were minor restrictions on the directors' powers that did not strip the hypothetical shareholder of de jure control (paragraph 87), and it decided the appeal on the director-election provisions of paragraph 3.2, under which non-residents could elect only 3 of 7 directors in 2004 and from January 1 to July 21, 2005, and 4 of 8 directors from July 22, 2005; separately, Paragraph 13.1 of the USA required approval by holders of at least 75% of the issued Voting Shares for certain fundamental matters, a threshold above the non-residents' 62.52% (December 31, 2004) and 70.42% (December 31, 2005) holdings. Equally important, although Bagtech did not address the point, practitioners should consider that if a USA permits holders of a simple majority or two-thirds of the voting shares to amend or terminate it, a hypothetical non-resident shareholder holding 70.42% of the shares could arguably repeal the USA and elect a new Board, which may leave that shareholder a way to exercise effective control analogous to the Buckerfield's test and thus preserve de jure control under item (5) of paragraph 85 of Duha Printers.
Statutory Deeming Fictions, Contingent Rights, and De Facto Control Exposures

While the Crown in Bagtech litigated the reassessment exclusively under the de jure control standard of paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA—and notably did not argue the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) under section 245 of the ITA—the broader statutory framework of the ITA contains adjacent anti-avoidance and control rules that routinely disqualify foreign-backed SR&ED claimants. First, under paragraph 251(5)(b) of the ITA (which applies expressly to the definition of "Canadian-controlled private corporation" in subsection 125(7)), where at any time a person has a right under a contract, in equity or otherwise, either immediately or in the future and either absolutely or contingently, to acquire shares of the capital stock of a corporation or to control the voting rights of such shares—or to cause a corporation to redeem, acquire, or cancel any shares of its capital stock owned by other shareholders (except where the right is contingent on the death, bankruptcy, or permanent disability of an individual)—that person is deemed to occupy the same position in relation to the control of the corporation as if the person owned the shares or caused the redemption at that time. Consequently, uncapped convertible debentures, stock options, warrants, or shotgun buy-sell clauses held by non-resident investors can trigger non-CCPC status if the newly issued or surviving shares would alter Board election control or cross a USA termination threshold.

Second, paragraph 125(7)(a) of the ITA disqualifies any corporation that is "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever" by one or more non-resident persons or public corporations. Pursuant to subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA, "controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever" incorporates de facto control (control in fact), which exists where a non-resident person or group of non-residents has any direct or indirect influence that, if exercised, would result in control in fact of the corporation. Even where a Bagtech-compliant USA prevents non-residents from exercising de jure control over the election of the Board under paragraph 125(7)(b), if the Canadian corporation is economically or operationally captive to a non-resident shareholder or strategic partner via demand debt facilities, exclusive technology supply, or operational vetoes, the CRA can challenge CCPC status under the de facto control prong of paragraph 125(7)(a).
Intersecting Substantive SR&ED Evidentiary and Contractual Pitfalls

In Canadian SR&ED practice, corporate CCPC disputes of the Bagtech variety rarely occur in isolation; when foreign venture capital or strategic corporate investors fund a Canadian R&D subsidiary, the CRA conducts a dual-track audit involving both a Financial Reviewer—examining CCPC status under subsection 125(7), qualified expenditures under subsection 37(1), and assistance or contract payments under subsection 127(9)—and a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) examining scientific eligibility under subsection 248(1) of the ITA. When non-resident strategic investors or corporate partners inject capital alongside commercial R&D contracts—such as research contracts of indeterminate duration where an investor or partner receives a percentage of future income from product sales (e.g., 10%) or licensing revenue (e.g., 25%) resulting from the R&D work—the CRA frequently scrutinizes whether the inflows constitute "non-government assistance" or a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Under the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), any SR&ED expenditure funded by a contract payment (where SR&ED is performed for or on behalf of another person) or government/non-government assistance reduces the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar, extinguishing the ITC claim regardless of whether the corporation successfully defends its CCPC status under Bagtech.

Simultaneously, on the substantive technical front, the taxpayer bears the legal burden of establishing that its claimed operating and capital expenditures ($1,017,722 operating and $431,517 capital in 2004; $1,461,189 operating and $69,641 capital in 2005 for Bagtech) satisfy the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Under the five-question jurisprudential test established by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839 (TCC)), the taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities that: (1) there was a genuine technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard practice; (2) the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; (3) the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through a structured process of systematic investigation or experimentation; (4) the process resulted in a technological advancement; and (5) a detailed, contemporaneous record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed. Failure to maintain contemporaneous laboratory, clinical, or software engineering records linking specific experimental hypotheses to general ledger cost pools will result in technical disqualification even where corporate CCPC control is impeccably structured.
Comparative Summary Table of Legal Requirements, Vulnerabilities, and Judicial Standards

The following table maps each statutory corporate, contractual, and technical SR&ED requirement implicated by Bagtech and the governing provisions of the Income Tax Act against the specific vulnerabilities challenged by the Crown and the evidentiary standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer Vulnerability / Crown Challenge in Bagtech & SR&ED Audits
Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof & Judicial Holding

cells: Hypothetical Shareholder Aggregation Test
ITA s. 125(7) definition of CCPC, para. (b); Sedona Networks Corp. v. The Queen, 2007 FCA 169

Non-residents owned >60% (2004) and 70.42% (2005) of Bagtech's voting Class A shares. The Crown argued that aggregating these shares into a single "particular person" automatically conferred arithmetic de jure control.

Two-Stage Legal Reality Standard: Stage 1 aggregates all non-resident and public corporation shares into one hypothetical person; Stage 2 evaluates whether that person holds de jure control while remaining bound by the legal rights and USA restrictions attached to those shares under CBCA s. 146(3) (R. v. Verrette).
Constitutional Validity of a Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement (USA)
CBCA s. 146(1)–(3) vs. s. 145.1; Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 795, para. 85

The Crown argued primarily that a USA cannot be taken into consideration at all at Stage 2; the Court then examined, in light of doctrine and Leblanc v. Fertek Inc. treating USAs as severable, whether Articles 3.1 and 3.2 (electing directors by shareholder groups A, B, and C) could be considered, or only the clauses restricting the directors' powers under CBCA s. 146(1).

Hybrid Constitutional Standard: The taxpayer must prove through a written agreement signed by all shareholders (voting and non-voting) that the agreement genuinely restricts the directors' statutory powers to manage the corporation (as identified by the Court in Appendix 3 of Bagtech, which it characterized as minor restrictions). Once established as a valid s. 146(1) USA, its board-election limits bind the de jure control analysis.
Restriction of Majority Shareholder's Power to Elect the Board
ITA s. 125(7)(b); Buckerfield's Ltd., 64 DTC 5301; Duha Printers, para. 85
Non-resident investors outnumbered Canadian residents in Class A shareholdings, creating a prima facie presumption that non-residents could elect the entire Board of Directors.

Effective Majority Election Test: The taxpayer must demonstrate that under the constating documents or a valid USA, the hypothetical non-resident shareholder is legally incapable of electing more than 50% of the Board (Bagtech's non-residents could elect only 3 of 7 directors in 2004 and from January 1 to July 21, 2005, and 4 of 8 from July 22, 2005).
Protection Against Unilateral USA Amendment or Ordinary Resolution Override
CBCA s. 146(1), s. 2(1); USA Paragraphs 13.1 & 13.4
The Crown contended that because many USA clauses were implemented by ordinary resolution, the non-resident majority retained de jure control over corporate affairs.

No Separate Standard Articulated: The Court did not rule separately on this argument; it found that the clauses restricting the directors' powers (Appendix 3) were minor restrictions that did not strip the hypothetical shareholder of de jure control (para. 87) and decided the appeal on the director-election provisions of the USA. The reasons make no finding that a supermajority threshold is required (Para. 13.1's 75% threshold is noted only as a provision in the nature of a USA under CBCA s. 6(3)) and none on the amendment or termination of the USA.
Absence of Contingent Control Rights and De Facto Control

Foreign venture capital financings frequently include convertible debt, warrants, redemption rights, or operational vetoes that deem non-residents to own additional voting shares or confer de facto control.

Deemed Exercise & Direct/Indirect Influence Standard: The taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities that no unexercised contractual right under s. 251(5)(b) would allow non-residents to capture a Board majority, and that foreign investors hold no coercive economic or operational leverage amounting to control in fact under s. 256(5.1).
Absence of Disqualifying Contract Payments or Assistance
ITA s. 127(9) ("qualified expenditure", "contract payment", "non-government assistance"), s. 127(18)–(20)
Foreign strategic investors often pair equity subscriptions with R&D service mandates or future product/licence revenue splits, risking recharacterization as funded research.

Economic Risk & Beneficial Ownership Standard: The taxpayer must prove through written contracts that equity subscriptions are strictly on capital account, that the Canadian performer retains beneficial ownership or autonomous exploitation rights to the resulting IP, and that no third party contracted for the specific SR&ED work.
Technological Uncertainty, Systematic Investigation, and Contemporaneous Evidence
ITA s. 248(1) ("scientific research and experimental development"), s. 37(1); Northwest Hydraulic, 98 DTC 1839

Absent verified scientific eligibility and auditable cost segregation ($1.017M operating / $431K capital in 2004; $1.461M operating / $69K capital in 2005), CCPC status yields zero refundable tax credits.

Five-Question Contemporaneous Proof Standard: The taxpayer must adduce dated, contemporaneous technical records proving (1) technological uncertainty, (2) explicit hypotheses, (3) systematic experimentation, (4) technological advancement, and (5) a permanent record of hypotheses tested and results tied to T661/Schedule 31 financial ledgers.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To illustrate how Canadian technology corporations and their legal and tax advisors can proactively engineer around the corporate, contractual, and technical traps identified in Bagtech (2012 TCC 120), the following two industry case studies set out comprehensive, step-by-step remedial architectures.
Case Study 1: Cross-Border Venture-Backed Biopolymer and Medical Device Developer
Baseline Scenario and Diagnostic Pitfall Analysis

BioHydrogel MedTech Inc. ("BioHydrogel") is a Montreal-based corporation incorporated under the CBCA that develops injectable, thermo-responsive chitosan-alginate hydrogels for osteochondral tissue regeneration, operating in the same biomedical hydrogel sector as Bagtech. In its current taxation year, BioHydrogel incurs $2,400,000 in SR&ED salaries, materials consumed, and specialized rheometer capital expenditures, seeking $840,000 in federal refundable SR&ED ITCs at the 35% CCPC rate under subsections 127(10.1) and 127.1(1) of the ITA. Following a Series B financing led by two Boston-based healthcare venture capital funds and a Swiss pharmaceutical corporate venture arm, non-residents collectively hold 68% of BioHydrogel's single class of Class A voting common shares, while the Canadian resident founders and a Quebec institutional venture fund hold the remaining 32%. One retired Canadian co-founder also holds 100 non-voting Class D preferred shares issued at incorporation in exchange for patent assignments.

To preserve Canadian representation on the Board of Directors, the Class A common shareholders signed a two-page "Voting Trust and Board Nomination Agreement" providing that the Canadian founders and the Quebec institutional fund will nominate three of the five directors and the non-resident investors will nominate two of the five directors, but the retired holder of the non-voting Class D preferred shares was never asked to sign the document. Furthermore, the two-page agreement contains no provisions restricting the powers of the directors to manage the business and affairs of the corporation. Simultaneously, the Swiss corporate investor signed a "Collaborative R&D Option Agreement" advancing $500,000 in milestone payments in exchange for an exclusive right to take title to the hydrogel formulations upon successful animal trials. On the laboratory floor, BioHydrogel's biochemists track formulation adjustments informally in shared spreadsheets without recording baseline rheological thresholds or failed cross-linking hypotheses.

A diagnostic review under Bagtech and the ITA reveals three fatal defects. First, the two-page "Voting Trust and Board Nomination Agreement" fails to qualify as a Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA on two independent grounds: it was not signed by all shareholders of the corporation (having omitted the holder of the non-voting Class D shares), and it contains no constitutional clauses restricting the powers of the directors to manage the corporation's business and affairs, rendering it a mere private voting agreement under section 145.1 of the CBCA. Under Duha Printers and Bagtech, the CRA will disregard this agreement entirely at Stage 2 of the Sedona Networks test, attribute 68% of the voting shares to the hypothetical non-resident "particular person" under paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA, and deny CCPC status. Second, the $500,000 milestone funding from the Swiss investor constitutes a "contract payment" or "non-government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA because the Swiss entity receives direct contractual rights to acquire the R&D outputs, reducing BioHydrogel's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar. Third, the informal spreadsheet tracking lacks a hypothesis-driven experimental structure and fails to separate routine formulation optimization from genuine technological uncertainty under subsection 248(1) of the ITA.
Step 1: Corporate Governance and Constitutional Share and USA Restructuring

To insulate BioHydrogel's CCPC status against both an initial CRA desk-audit arithmetic screen and a substantive Bagtech legal review, corporate and tax counsel must execute a dual-layer constitutional restructuring prior to the commencement of the taxation year, as subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA requires the taxpayer to qualify as a CCPC throughout the entire taxation year. Counsel must first replace the two-page voting agreement with a comprehensive Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement executed by 100% of all shareholders of the corporation, explicitly including the Canadian resident founders, the Quebec institutional fund, all non-resident Series B investors, and the retired co-founder holding the non-voting Class D shares. Articles 3.1 and 3.2 of the new USA must fix the Board of Directors at seven members allocated across three defined shareholder groups mirroring the victorious structure in Bagtech: Group A (composed of the Canadian resident founders, electing two directors), Group B (composed of the Quebec institutional fund and one foreign VC fund, wherein the Canadian fund holds the exclusive right to appoint two directors and the foreign VC fund appoints one director), and Group C (composed of the remaining non-resident investors, appointing two directors). This ensures that when all non-resident shares are notionally aggregated into a single hypothetical "particular person" at Stage 1 of the Sedona Networks test under paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA, that hypothetical person is legally restricted by the USA (and deemed bound under subsection 146(3) of the CBCA) to electing only three out of seven directors (42.86%), preventing the non-residents from acquiring de jure control.

To guarantee that the Tax Court of Canada recognizes the agreement as a constitutional USA under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA rather than a severable section 145.1 voting contract, the USA must explicitly incorporate the management-restricting architecture validated in Appendix 3 of Bagtech. Specifically, the USA must divest the directors of their statutory authority to elect the Chair of the Board, mandating that a designated Canadian resident Group A nominee serve as Chair; mandate at least six Board meetings per year spaced no more than two months apart; require the presence of at least one director appointed by each of Group A, Group B, and Group C to constitute a valid Board quorum; and withdraw the directors' powers to issue new securities, authorize share transfers outside prescribed parameters, or alter the core biomedical R&D mandate without prior shareholder authorization. Crucially, to neutralize the Crown's alternative argument in Bagtech regarding ordinary resolutions, the USA must stipulate that any management power withdrawn from the Board and vested in the shareholders requires a 75% supermajority vote of all voting shares (exceeding the non-residents' 68% ownership) plus the affirmative concurrence of a majority of the Canadian-resident Group A and Group B shareholders. The USA must also contain an entrenched amendment clause confirming that the agreement cannot be amended or terminated without 100% unanimous shareholder consent, and all share certificates must bear a conspicuous legend referencing the USA, since subsection 146(4) of the CBCA otherwise allows a transferee who was not informed of the USA, by an endorsement on the share certificate or otherwise, to rescind the acquisition (subsection 146(3) deeming every purchaser or transferee of shares to be a party to the USA). Finally, as a belt-and-suspenders measure, BioHydrogel should file Articles of Amendment under the CBCA to embed the Group A, Group B, and Group C class-specific director election rights directly into the Articles of Incorporation, thereby satisfying Duha Printers on the face of the charter documents as well as the USA.
Step 2: Contractual and Financial Restructuring to Eliminate Funded Research Exclusions

To prevent the $500,000 injection from the Swiss corporate venture arm from reducing BioHydrogel's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool under subsection 127(9) of the ITA or creating de facto control exposure under paragraph 125(7)(a) and subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA, the "Collaborative R&D Option Agreement" must be formally rescinded and replaced prior to the expenditure of the funds. In its place, the Swiss investor should subscribe for $500,000 of non-voting Class B preferred shares on pure capital account, carrying a non-cumulative dividend at a maximum rate of 8% and redeemable for its stated capital solely at the option of the corporation (the dividend and redemption-amount attributes matching the Class B shares in Bagtech and avoiding any holder-initiated redemption or conversion rights that could trigger paragraph 251(5)(b) of the ITA).

Concurrently, to address the Swiss investor's commercial interest without tainting the SR&ED claim as a "contract payment," BioHydrogel and the Swiss investor should execute an arm's-length "Right of First Negotiation and Future Licensing Protocol" patterned on commercial revenue-sharing structures accepted in Canadian tax law. Under this protocol, BioHydrogel retains 100% legal and beneficial ownership of all hydrogel intellectual property, patents, and experimental data, bears 100% of the financial risk of failed animal trials, and retains full autonomy to direct the scientific program, while granting the Swiss investor a commercial option—exercisable only after completion of the SR&ED phase—to negotiate a royalty-bearing distribution licence (e.g., paying BioHydrogel 10% of product sales and 25% of sub-licensing income). Because the $500,000 is received strictly as share capital consideration and no party has contracted for the performance of SR&ED on its behalf, the entire $2,400,000 SR&ED expenditure pool remains eligible for the 35% refundable ITC.
Step 3: Technical Documentation Architecture for Biomedical Hydrogel SR&ED Eligibility

To ensure that BioHydrogel's hydrogel formulation work satisfies the CRA's Research and Technology Advisor under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and is distinguished from routine formulation optimization, the Chief Scientific Officer must implement a mandatory SR&ED technical documentation architecture. For Technological Uncertainty (Form T661, Line 242), the research leads must author a baseline "Formulation Constraint Specification" at the outset of the taxation year explaining why existing chitosan-alginate and other thermo-responsive hydrogel systems cannot simultaneously achieve rapid in-situ gelation (sol-gel transition time < 45 seconds at 37 °C), high mechanical load-bearing capacity (compressive modulus ≥ 1 MPa), and shear-thinning injectability through a 25-gauge arthroscopic needle without inducing cytotoxic leaching of cross-linking reagents.

In documenting Systematic Investigation and Experimentation (Form T661, Line 244), each experimental series must be initiated by a dated "Protocol and Hypothesis Record" inside BioHydrogel's Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN). Each record must state a falsifiable scientific hypothesis (for example, hypothesizing that introducing a dual-stage enzymatic-ionic cross-linking mechanism using microbial transglutaminase and chelated calcium ions at molar ratios between 0.5:1 and 2:1 will decouple shear-viscosity during injection from post-injection storage modulus (G′) build-up), define the exact controlled variables across hydrogel batches (BH-2026-01 through BH-2026-24), and archive the resulting oscillatory rheometry curves (storage modulus G′, loss modulus G″, and complex viscosity η*), swelling-degradation kinetics, and in-vitro chondrocyte viability assays. In documenting Technological Advancement (Form T661, Line 246), the ELN synthesis must capture the new scientific knowledge generated from both failed and successful formulations—such as identifying an unexpected phase-separation boundary above 20 mM divalent cation concentration that causes brittle syneresis—thereby proving that the work advanced biopolymer materials science rather than routine product calibration.
Step 4: Experimentation and Financial Tracking Governance

To link the technical records seamlessly to the financial schedules on Form T661 and Schedule 31 (in Bagtech, the parties admitted in their agreed statement of facts that Bagtech incurred $1,017,722 in SR&ED operating expenses and $431,517 in SR&ED capital expenditures in 2004, and $1,461,189 and $69,641, respectively, in 2005), BioHydrogel must configure its enterprise resource planning (ERP) ledger with dedicated SR&ED project sub-accounts. All researchers must complete mandatory bi-weekly electronic time-sheets allocating their hours across specific experimental hypothesis codes (HYP-2026-01 through HYP-2026-08) corroborated by dated ELN entries, while non-SR&ED activities—such as Health Canada regulatory submissions, patent drafting, and commercial scale-up—are isolated in excluded cost centers. Destructive test batches of raw biopolymers are tracked via automated laboratory inventory logs to substantiate "materials consumed or transformed" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, ensuring an audit-ready evidentiary trail across both financial and scientific reviews.
Case Study 2: Foreign-Partnered Industrial AI and Autonomous Robotics Enterprise
Baseline Scenario and Diagnostic Pitfall Analysis

AutonoSense Robotics Corp. ("AutonoSense") is a Waterloo, Ontario corporation governed by the CBCA that develops solid-state LiDAR and neuromorphic vision sensor-fusion architectures for autonomous underground mining vehicles. In its current taxation year, AutonoSense incurs $2,850,000 in software engineering and robotics R&D operating and capital expenditures, claiming $997,500 in refundable federal SR&ED ITCs at the 35% CCPC rate. AutonoSense's Class A voting common shares are owned 48% by its three Canadian resident founders, 32% by a Delaware venture capital fund, and 20% by a publicly traded German industrial robotics manufacturer. Because paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA aggregates shares owned by both non-resident persons and public corporations into the single hypothetical "particular person," the hypothetical person holds 52% of AutonoSense's voting shares. Furthermore, the German public corporation holds convertible debentures that, if converted, would increase the combined non-resident and public corporation voting share ownership to 65%.

To address corporate governance, the shareholders signed a Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement providing for a six-member Board of Directors, under which the Canadian founders elect three directors, the Delaware VC fund elects two directors, and the German public corporation elects one director. However, the USA contains three critical drafting flaws: first, it grants the Chair of the Board—who is appointed by the Delaware VC fund—a casting (second) tie-breaking vote in the event of a 3-3 deadlock on the Board; second, it provides that all matters withdrawn from the Board's authority under the USA shall be decided by an "ordinary resolution of the Shareholders"; and third, its amendment clause permits the USA to be amended or terminated by a two-thirds (66.67%) vote of the voting shares. Additionally, AutonoSense performs 30% of its sensor-fusion testing under a "Master Engineering Services Agreement" (MESA) for a Canadian mining customer that pays AutonoSense time-and-materials engineering fees, while AutonoSense's software developers track their work using standard commercial Agile Jira tickets (e.g., "Fix LiDAR point-cloud latency bug") without documenting algorithmic uncertainty or systematic experimentation.

A diagnostic audit under Bagtech and the ITA exposes four disqualifying failures. First, although the non-resident VC fund and German public corporation elect only three of the six directors (50%), granting a casting tie-breaking vote to the Chair appointed by the Delaware VC fund hands legal control of the Board of Directors to the hypothetical non-resident/public corporation "particular person" under paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA. Second, because the hypothetical person holds 52% of the voting shares directly—and is deemed by paragraph 251(5)(b) of the ITA to own 65% of the voting shares via the German corporation's convertible debentures—allowing USA shareholder decisions to be made by "ordinary resolution" (50% + 1) triggers the Crown's alternative argument in Bagtech by vesting management control directly in the foreign/public majority. Moreover, if the convertible debentures are supplemented by even a small anti-dilution warrant that pushes deemed non-resident/public ownership to 66.67%, the hypothetical person could unilaterally terminate the USA under the two-thirds amendment clause. Third, the time-and-materials payments under the MESA constitute a disqualifying "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Fourth, the commercial bug-fix Jira tickets fail to substantiate scientific or technological uncertainty under subsection 248(1) of the ITA.
Step 1: Corporate Governance, USA, and Convertible Security Restructuring

To restore CCPC eligibility under paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA and align AutonoSense's governance with the Tax Court of Canada's holding in Bagtech, corporate counsel must immediately amend and restate the Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA. First, Articles 3.1 and 3.2 of the USA must be amended to eliminate the non-resident Chair's casting vote entirely and either (a) expand the Board to seven directors—allocating four directors to the Canadian resident founders (Group A) and three directors combined to the Delaware VC fund (Group B, two directors) and the German public corporation (Group C, one director)—or (b) maintain an eight-director or six-director even split (matching Bagtech's 4-of-8 split after the July 22, 2005 amendment) where no Chair or director holds a tie-breaking vote and the Chair is appointed exclusively by the Canadian resident founders. Because de jure control under Buckerfield's, Duha Printers, and Bagtech requires the legal power to elect a majority (more than 50%) of the Board of Directors, capping the hypothetical non-resident/public corporation "particular person" at 42.86% (3 of 7) or 50.00% (3 of 6 or 4 of 8 without a casting vote) deprives the hypothetical person of de jure control.

Second, the USA must retain genuine management-restricting clauses under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA (such as quorum rules requiring at least one director from each of Group A, Group B, and Group C, mandatory bi-monthly Board meetings, and restrictions on share transfers and security issuances as validated in Appendix 3 of Bagtech), while replacing all "ordinary resolution" shareholder implementation thresholds with an 80% supermajority voting threshold that also requires the separate written consent of the Canadian resident Group A founders. The two-thirds amendment clause must be repealed and replaced with a contractual unanimity requirement (100% of all shareholders) for any amendment, waiver, or termination of the USA. Third, to neutralize paragraph 251(5)(b) of the ITA, the German public corporation's convertible debentures must be amended so that they are convertible exclusively into non-voting Class C participating shares, or alternatively, the USA must expressly stipulate pursuant to subsection 146(3) of the CBCA that any Class A shares issued upon conversion of the debentures are automatically bound by Group C of the USA and carry zero right to increase Group C's fixed allocation of one director or override the 80% / Group A veto thresholds.
Step 2: Commercial Contract Restructuring to Preserve SR&ED Expenditure Pools

To prevent the revenue from the Canadian mining customer from disqualifying AutonoSense's sensor-fusion R&D under the "contract payment" exclusion in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, AutonoSense must terminate the blended Master Engineering Services Agreement and bifurcate its customer dealings into two legally distinct contracts. Under the first contract—a "Commercial Hardware Mounting and Site Calibration Agreement"—AutonoSense bills strictly for routine field installation and sensor calibration services performed by field technicians; all salaries and costs associated with this contract are segregated into a commercial general ledger code and excluded from Form T661. Under the second contract—a "Standard Post-Development Software Subscription Licence"—AutonoSense grants the customer a non-exclusive licence to use compiled binary releases of AutonoSense's proprietary perception platform for a fixed annual subscription fee, while explicitly stipulating that all underlying neuromorphic sensor-fusion R&D is self-initiated, self-directed, and funded at AutonoSense's sole risk, with 100% of all intellectual property vesting unconditionally in AutonoSense. This contractual wall ensures that no portion of the $2,850,000 R&D budget is performed "for or on behalf of" the customer under subsection 127(9) of the ITA.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Algorithmic and Systems-Level Uncertainty

To satisfy the CRA's Research and Technology Advisor under subsection 248(1) of the ITA that AutonoSense's development work transcends routine software engineering and debugging, the Chief Technology Officer must implement a mandatory SR&ED technical documentation architecture. For Technological Uncertainty (Form T661, Line 242), technical leads must author a baseline "System Architecture Constraint Specification" at the outset of the fiscal year explaining why state-of-the-art Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) frameworks (such as Extended Kalman Filters and iterative closest-point LiDAR registration) break down in subterranean mining tunnels characterized by self-similar rock wall geometry, heavy airborne particulate occlusion (dust densities above 10 mg/m³ scattering 905 nm laser pulses), and strict edge-processor thermal limits (≤ 15 W TDP). The specification must define the exact technological uncertainty: whether asynchronous, microsecond-resolution event streams from a neuromorphic vision sensor can be mathematically fused with sparse solid-state LiDAR returns within a continuous-time state estimator to bound localization drift below 10 cm per 100 m travelled at 200 Hz update rates without exceeding onboard L2 cache bandwidth.

For Systematic Investigation (Form T661, Line 244), software engineering sprints must be organized around formal "Experimental Hypothesis Tickets" rather than commercial feature stories. Each investigation must document the specific mathematical or algorithmic hypothesis tested (for example, hypothesizing that replacing dense 3D voxel-grid convolutions with a continuous-time spatio-temporal graph neural network that prunes edges dynamically via Poisson spike-timing-dependent plasticity will reduce memory bandwidth saturation by 65% while preserving sub-centimeter pose estimation under simulated Mie-scattering dust occlusion), the synthetic and underground test-rig datasets executed, and the quantitative benchmark metrics (root-mean-square trajectory error, 99th-percentile inference latency, and L2 cache miss rates) that falsified or validated each iteration. For Technological Advancement (Form T661, Line 246), the engineering logs must synthesize the generalizable algorithmic knowledge gained from failed neural topologies and numerical instabilities.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Agile Experimentation and Financial Tracking

To establish an unassailable contemporaneous nexus between the software experimentation and the $2,850,000 SR&ED cost pool, AutonoSense must integrate its engineering repositories directly with its accounting controls. Developers must tag all experimental Git commits, pull requests, and MLOps training runs (in MLflow or Weights & Biases) with structured metadata identifiers ([SRED-PROJ-01][HYP-2026-03]), automatically archiving timestamped commit diffs, failed convergence graphs, and telemetry logs as permanent contemporaneous evidence. Simultaneously, AutonoSense's Jira environment must be partitioned into two segregated workflows: ENG-PROD (capturing routine UI coding, customer site integration, and commercial bug fixes) and SRED-EXP (capturing time spent designing, executing, and analyzing experimental hypothesis iterations). By linking the SRED-EXP time-tracking ledger directly to payroll T4 wage allocations and capital test-bench depreciation schedules under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the ITA, AutonoSense ensures full compliance with both the substantive scientific standards of the Tax Court of Canada and the corporate CCPC governance rules established in Bagtech.

outcome: Appeal allowed; TCC held the company remained a CCPC and was entitled to the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED tax credit.
